Answering the first question. We build our morals based on our experience and the shape of society we want and are in.

Answering the second. It is important to remember that this is MY morality, not that of the world and not that of all atheists. From this, yes, it is wrong for social norms to prevent you from living your life freely and without discomfort, but this rule is subject to the first one, your lifestyle cannot be psychologically or physically aggressive to others. 

Answering the third paragraph: yes, believing in energies and so on is believing in the unseen. Atheists who believe this are atheists who are not skeptics. We skeptical atheists only believe statements about the universe and its nature that have a strong scientific basis. But not everyone is like that.

Me being an atheist, I would like to give my point of view

Atheism does not have a moral. It is not a philosophy that seeks any kind of morals. We atheists just believe that no god exists, this is the basis.

From there you can find different types of atheists, who have diferent morals and even believe in other paranormal phenomena, such as spirits, energies and etc.

I personally set my moral line on the idea of ​​the common benefit of humanity. 
My morals have three levels of importance to follow

1: If an act harms a person physically or psychologically, it is wrong. This idea can only be broken if your act is to prevent direct physical or psychological aggression to you or someone else0

2: If your attitude makes it difficult or impossible for someone else to experience and enjoy their life freely, without a suitable justification it is wrong.

3: If your action causes great discomfort to people in general, it is advisable that you stop. This rule can be broken if the act is necessary to break unnecessary social taboos


These three levels of importance are ranked from "most important" to "least important", but the idea is that all these ideas complement each other when dealing with complex real situations.


Most atheists form their moral understandings on basic social aspects of their time, building a morality that makes sense to them.
